lesson.title: Two Distributions Walk Into a Classroom: Comparing Shape, Center, and Spread
lesson.summary: Comparing distributions means describing shape, outliers, center, and spread for each group in context, using tools like parallel boxplots, histograms, means, and standard deviations rather than looking at a single number in isolation.
lesson.body:
Statistics rarely asks you to describe just one group. Far more often, the interesting question is how two or more groups differ: did one teaching method outperform another, does one factory's parts vary less than a competitor's, is one town's commute time typically shorter than another's? Answering questions like these requires comparing distributions, and doing it well means addressing four things every time: shape, outliers, center, and spread, sometimes remembered by the acronym SOCS. Crucially, every comparison must be made in context and in complete sentences, using words like higher, lower, more spread out, or more consistent, not just listing numbers side by side.

Shape describes whether a distribution is roughly symmetric or skewed, and whether it has one main peak or several. A histogram is usually the clearest tool for judging shape, since a boxplot can hide the presence of multiple peaks. Outliers are unusual values that stand apart from the rest of the data, visible as isolated dots beyond a boxplot's whiskers or as points sitting far from the bulk of a histogram. Center is typically summarized by the mean or the median, and spread by the standard deviation, the range, or the interquartile range, with the choice depending on shape: the median and IQR resist skew and outliers, while the mean and standard deviation are the natural pair to report when a distribution is fairly symmetric.

Suppose two sections of the same statistics exam produce these five-number summaries. Section A, with 30 students: minimum 45, Q1 62, median 71, Q3 80, maximum 95, mean 70.2, standard deviation 12.6. Section B, with 28 students: minimum 58, Q1 74, median 79, Q3 85, maximum 99, mean 78.9, standard deviation 8.1. Comparing centers, Section B's median of 79 is 8 points higher than Section A's median of 71, and Section B's mean tells the same story, sitting 8.7 points higher than Section A's mean. Comparing spread, Section A's IQR is 80 minus 62, or 18 points, while Section B's IQR is 85 minus 74, or 11 points, and Section A's standard deviation of 12.6 is likewise noticeably larger than Section B's 8.1.

Put into a full sentence, as an AP Statistics response should be: Section B typically scored higher than Section A, since both its median and mean exceed Section A's by roughly 8 points, and Section B's scores were also more consistent, since both its IQR and standard deviation are smaller, indicating less variability around its center. Neither section shows an obvious outlier from the five-number summaries alone, though a boxplot or histogram of the raw scores would be needed to confirm that and to compare shape directly.

This kind of comparison is the payoff for everything built up through quartiles, the five-number summary, boxplots, means, and standard deviations. None of those tools is very interesting in isolation. Their real value shows up here, when two groups need to be placed side by side and described honestly, in the actual context of the data, rather than reduced to a single number that hides whether the difference in center is large relative to how much the groups naturally vary.
